d: 1. (Bot.) “The deadly nightshade (Atropa Belladonna), having stupefying qualities.”
2. (Her.) “The tincture sable or black when blazoned according to the fantastic system in which plants are substituted for the tinctures.”
3. A sleeping potion; an opiate. Chaucer.
w.e: OE. dwale, dwole, deception, deadly nightshade, AS. dwala, dwola, error, doubt; akin to E. dull. See Dull, a.

d: 1. (Carp.) “A piece of wood set between two studs, posts, etc., to stiffen and support them.”
2. (Mech.) (a) A kind of crowbar. (b) A large wrench. Knight.
w.e: Cf. D. dwingen to force, compel.
OE. dwergh, dwerf, dwarf, AS. dweorg, dweorh; akin to D. dwerg, MHG. twerc, G. zwerg, Icel. dvergr, Sw. & Dan. dverg; of unknown origin.

d: To hinder from growing to the natural size; to make or keep small; to stunt. Addison. Even the most common moral ideas and affections . . . would be stunted and dwarfed, if cut off from a spiritual background. J. C. Shairp.
To become small; to diminish in size. Strange power of the world that, the moment we enter it, our great conceptions dwarf. Beaconsfield.

n: a plant or animal that is atypically small
a person who is markedly small
the lack of sunlight dwarfed these pines
a legendary creature resembling a tiny old man
This year's debt dwarfs that of last year

d: Like a dwarf; below the common stature or size; very small; petty; as, a dwarfish animal, shrub. -- Dwarfish*ly, adv. -- Dwarfish*ness, n.
A diminutive dwarf.
Much undersized. [R.] Waterhouse.
Dwaule, v. i. “To be delirious. [Obs.] Junius.”
Dwaule, v. i. “To be delirious. [Obs.] Junius.”
1. To delay; to linger. [Obs.]
2. To abide; to remain; to continue. I 'll rather dwell in my necessity. Shak. Thy soul was like a star and dwelt apart. Wordsworth.

3. To abide as a permanent resident, or for a time; to live in a place; to reside. The parish in which I was born, dwell, and have possessions. Peacham. The poor man dwells in a humble cottage near the hall where the lord of the domain resides. C. J. Smith. To dwell in, to abide in (a place); hence, to depend on. My hopes in heaven to dwell. Shak. -- To dwel
w.e: OE. dwellen, dwelien, to err, linger, AS. dwellan to deceive, hinder, delay, dwelian to err; akin to Icel. dvelja to delay, tarry, Sw. dväljas to dwell, Dan. dvæle to linger, and to E. dull. See Dull,

d: To inhabit. [R.] Milton.

n: The problems dwell in the social injustices in this country
think moodily or anxiously about something
be an inhabitant of or reside in
People lived in Africa millions of years ago

d: An inhabitant; a resident; as, a cave dweller. Dwellers at Jerusalem. Acts i. 19.

n: a person who inhabits a particular place

d: Habitation; place or house in which a person lives; abode; domicile. Hazor shall be a dwelling for dragons. Jer. xlix. 33. God will deign To visit oft the dwellings of just men. Milton. Philip's dwelling fronted on the street. Tennyson. Dwelling house, a house intended to be occupied as a residence, in distinction from a store, office, or other building. --

n: housing that someone is living in
he built a modest dwelling near the pond

d: of Dwell.

To diminish; to become less; to shrink; to waste or consume away; to become degenerate; to fall away. Weary sennights nine times nine Shall he dwindle, peak and pine. Shak. Religious societies, though begun with excellent intentions, are said to have dwindled into factious clubs. Swift.
w.e: From OE. dwinen to languish, waste away, AS. dwinan; akin to LG. dwinen, D. dwijnen to vanish, Icel. dvina to cease, dwindle, Sw. tvina; of uncertain origin. The suffix -le, preceded by d excrescent a

d: 1. To make less; to bring low. Our drooping days are dwindled down to naught. Thomson.
2. To break; to disperse. [R.] Clarendon.
The process of dwindling; dwindlement; decline; degeneracy. [R.] Johnson.
The act or process of dwindling; a dwindling. [R.] Mrs. Oliphant.
To waste away; to pine; to languish. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] Gower.

n: a genetic abnormality resulting in short stature
there is no greater sadness that the dwindling away of a family
an insignificant student who is ridiculed as being affected or boringly studious
